opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the questions people ask me most, and my honest answer is that both are really valuable and you probably want good people in both places. But they have different comparative advantages.

Inside a frontier lab, the big advantage is access. You're closer to the models while they're being trained, you can see the full training pipeline, you might have access to internal reasoning or model internals that external parties don't get, and you can actually influence what happens before deployment. If you find a problem, you're right there to help fix it. And frankly, a lot of the most important mitigation work, like changing training so models scheme less in the first place, basically has to happen inside the labs, because that's where the training happens.

On the other side, being external gives you a few things that are hard to replicate internally. One is independence. If you're at Apollo and you find something concerning, you're not in a position where your employer's commercial interests are directly tied to the result. That matters both for how you actually do the work and for how credible the findings are to outsiders, like policymakers or the public. Another is breadth. We work with multiple labs, so we see patterns across models and can say "this isn't a quirk of one company, this is a general phenomenon." And third, there's a sort of ecosystem-building role: an external organisation can develop evaluation methods, publish them, push for norms, and help set up what third-party assessment should look like, which I think will matter more and more as these systems get more capable.

There are trade-offs, of course. Externally, you're often working with less access and under time pressure before a release, and you depend on labs being willing to cooperate. Internally, you have to be honest with yourself about incentives and about whether you'll be able to raise concerns effectively when it counts.

So the way I'd frame it for someone deciding: if you're most excited about directly shaping how models are trained and you trust that you'd have real influence, a lab can be great. If you care about independent verification, building the science in a way that applies across the field, and having a voice that's credibly separate from any single developer, then external work is really important. And I'd say we need a healthy number of strong people on the external side, because right now that ecosystem is still quite small relative to how important I think it's going to be.

r001.rationale: The response says lab staff have direct access to models and the training pipeline, can influence training before deployment, and can help implement training changes to reduce scheming.

r002.rationale: It says working with multiple labs reveals patterns across models, but does not argue that this increases the external organisation’s chances of impact.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute an external organisation’s ability to move quickly to low organisational overhead.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the risk of achieving nothing at a small external organisation with that at a large organisation.

r005.rationale: The response calls both paths valuable and describes when each may suit someone; it does not judge external work as typically higher impact for someone willing to take risks.

r006.rationale: It describes independence from commercial interests and credibility with outsiders, but does not identify greater freedom to publicly express one’s views as an advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, partly because it's a question that people ask me when they're deciding where to apply, and partly because I had to make that call myself when we started Apollo.

The honest answer is that both are really valuable, and I don't think there's a universal "one is better than the other." It depends a lot on what you're trying to do and what kind of person you are.

Let me start with the case for the labs, because I think it's strong. If you're inside a frontier lab, you have access to the most capable models, you have access to the training process, you can actually change what goes into the model. If you want to reduce scheming, at some point someone has to actually do the training intervention — change the data, change the RL environment, change the spec, whatever it is. That lever only exists inside the lab. So if you're the kind of person who wants to be close to the thing that actually gets deployed, there's just no substitute. And frankly, the labs now have really good people working on this. It's not the case anymore that nobody internally cares about scheming or deceptive alignment. Several labs have dedicated teams on it now.

The case for external organisations is a bit different, and I'd break it into maybe three things.

The first is independence. When we evaluate a model and we say "this model showed scheming behaviour in these settings," there's no commercial incentive on our side to downplay it or to frame it in a way that makes a launch look okay. The lab might be totally honest — I think many of the people there are — but structurally, the incentives are different, and I think the world is better off having someone who can say the uncomfortable thing without worrying about the next funding round or the next product release. Part of the value of an external org is that it's credible precisely because it doesn't have skin in the game in the same way.

The second is that you can work across labs. We've run evaluations on models from multiple developers. That means you build up a cross-cutting picture: which behaviours are common to all frontier models, which are specific to a particular training setup. Inside a lab you typically only see your own models, and you often can't share what you see with the outside world, or only in very constrained ways. Externally, we can publish, we can compare, we can help set a bar that everybody has to clear.

The third is that external orgs can shape the ecosystem — norms, policy, what "good enough" evidence looks like before deployment. That's not really what a lab team is set up to do.

Now, the trade-offs. Externally, you have less access. You often get models late, or in restricted ways, or without the training details you'd really want. You can find a behaviour but you can't necessarily fix it; you have to hand it to someone else and hope they prioritise it. And there's just a lot less compute and infrastructure, so you spend time on things that a lab engineer would never think about.

And on the lab side, the main cost is that you're a small part of a very big organisation whose primary goal isn't safety. You might get pulled onto something else when the product deadline comes around. You might find yourself in a position where you see something concerning and your options for doing something about it are limited to internal escalation. And there's a subtle thing where the environment shapes your beliefs — if everyone around you thinks things are basically fine, it's hard to stay calibrated.

So, how would I weigh it for an individual? I'd ask: do you want to build the fix or do you want to find the problem and hold people accountable? Do you care more about direct impact on one model or on the bar that all models have to meet? And honestly: how do you personally handle incentive pressure? Some people are great at staying independent-minded inside a big organisation, and some people aren't, and it's worth being honest with yourself about which one you are.

My overall view is that we need both, and we need them talking to each other. The best outcome I've seen is when an external org finds something, the lab takes it seriously, and the next version is actually better. That loop doesn't work if either side is missing. So I don't think of it as competition — I think the question is really about where your particular skills and temperament push the loop forward the most.

r001.rationale: It says lab access to frontier models and training lets you make interventions that reduce scheming.

r002.rationale: It says external groups can evaluate models across developers, compare findings, and help set a bar for all labs.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute faster work to low organisational overhead.

r004.rationale: It mentions limited resources and relying on labs to act on findings, but does not say a small external organisation faces a higher risk of achieving nothing than a large organisation.

r005.rationale: The response says both paths are valuable and depend on the person; it does not judge external work to have higher expected impact for someone willing to take risks.

r006.rationale: It presents independence as an external advantage, including the ability to publish findings and say uncomfortable things without launch or funding pressures.

astra-6.text:
I think there are strong reasons to do both. Inside a frontier lab, you’re much closer to the models and the decisions that matter. You can study systems during training, work with the people building them, and potentially turn a research result into a change in how a model is trained or deployed. From outside, you can have a useful finding and still struggle to get it implemented.

The case for an external organisation like Apollo is independence. You can choose your research agenda, work across multiple labs, and challenge assumptions that might be shared within one company. And if your findings are inconvenient for a deployment decision, having some distance from the commercial incentives is valuable. Of course, being external doesn’t automatically make you independent in practice: you still need access, and that creates its own pressures.

So I wouldn’t frame it as one being universally better. We need people inside labs who can make changes, and external groups that can scrutinise the evidence and develop methods that aren’t tied to one company. For an individual, I’d look closely at the actual role: what access would you have, what could you investigate, and who would act on what you found? Those details can matter more than which side of the organisational boundary you sit on.

r001.rationale: It says people inside a lab are closer to its models and can potentially turn research into changes to training or deployment.

r002.rationale: It says an external group can work across multiple labs, but does not say this increases its chances of impact.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute an external organisation’s speed to low organisational overhead.

r004.rationale: It does not identify a higher risk of achieving nothing at a small external organisation than at a large one.

r005.rationale: It gives a balanced comparison without expressing Hobbhahn’s judgment that external work typically has higher expected impact for risk-tolerant people.

r006.rationale: It mentions independence and freedom to choose a research agenda, but not greater freedom to publicly express one’s views.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are real advantages to both. Inside a frontier lab, you have access to the models, the training process, and the people making decisions. If you find something concerning, you can potentially turn that directly into a change in how the model is trained or deployed. From the outside, you might identify a problem but have less ability to fix it.

The advantage of an external organisation is independence. You can work across multiple labs, compare what you’re seeing, and develop your own view of which questions matter. You’re also less exposed to the pressure within any one company to ship a particular model. That doesn’t mean people inside labs can’t do good safety work; it means the institutional incentives are different.

So I wouldn’t frame this as choosing the one correct place to do anti-scheming work. We need people inside labs who can actually implement mitigations, and external organisations that can scrutinise those mitigations and ask whether they work. And the external work is much more useful when there’s enough access and cooperation to test the systems that matter.

For an individual, I’d look closely at the specific role: what access will you have, how much freedom will you have to pursue concerning results, and who will act on what you find? Those details can matter more than whether the organisation is formally internal or external.

r002.rationale: It says external groups can work across multiple labs, but does not argue that this raises their chances of impact.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute an external organisation’s speed to low organisational overhead.

r004.rationale: It does not identify a higher risk of achieving nothing at a small external organisation.

r005.rationale: It gives no judgment that external anti-scheming work typically has higher expected impact for risk-tolerant people.

r006.rationale: It mentions independence from company pressure, but not greater freedom to publicly state one’s views.
